title: Command reference
intro: The commands you use every day as a platform engineer, each with what it does and an example you can copy. Examples use the lab's names (orders-app, lab-gitflow, rg-mfs-*) where it helps. Shell note: in Git Bash use forward slashes (/c/Projects/...); in PowerShell backslashes are fine.

sections.title: Azure CLI (az)
sections.note: On Windows az is a .cmd file: in PowerShell, expressions with parentheses or pipes in --query can break. Prefer counting and filtering in PowerShell (ConvertFrom-Json) or escape the quotes.

commands.what: Who you are and which subscription is active. Two subscriptions can share a name: target them by ID. -o table hides fields named id, so alias them (subId:id).
commands.example: az account list --query "[].{nome:name, subId:id, tenant:tenantId, padrao:isDefault}" -o table

commands.what: Changes the default subscription. Check it after any az login: logging in to another tenant can change it.
Runs one command against another subscription without changing the default — the safe way to look around.
Lists resource groups; managedBy shows groups owned by an Azure service (do not touch them).
commands.example: az group list --query "[].{rg:name, regiao:location, gerenciadoPor:managedBy}" -o table

commands.what: Lists resources, optionally in one group. Count them in PowerShell to avoid quoting problems with length().
Who has which role at which scope. --all lists every assignment in the subscription; --assignee filters by user or app.
commands.example: az role assignment list --assignee <your-upn> --all --query "[].{role:roleDefinitionName, scope:scope}" -o table

commands.what: Signs in to a specific tenant (directory). A token from one tenant does not reach subscriptions in another (MSAL cache error).

sections.title: Git
sections.note: Local version control. Everything here works in Azure Repos and GitHub alike.

commands.what: Shows the current branch, staged and unstaged changes and untracked files. Run it before and after every change.
Changes branch; -c creates a new one from a start point. Replaces the older git checkout for branches.
Stages changes for the next commit. -p lets you pick hunks interactively.
Records the staged changes with a message. Keep one logical change per commit.
commands.example: git commit -m "feat(orders): reject orders below the minimum value"

commands.what: Sends commits to a remote. -u sets the upstream so later pushes need no arguments.
Fetches and integrates the remote branch into yours. --rebase keeps history linear.
Downloads remote branches and tags without changing your working tree. --prune removes deleted remote branches.
Shows history. --oneline --graph is the quickest way to see how branches relate.
Shows changes: working tree vs index, --staged for what will be committed, or between two refs.
Joins another branch into the current one. --no-ff always creates a merge commit (useful for release/hotfix back-merges).
commands.example: git switch develop && git merge --no-ff release/1.0.0

commands.what: Replays your commits on top of another branch. Never rebase commits others already pulled.
Marks a commit, usually a release. Annotated tags (-a) carry author, date and message; push them explicitly.
commands.example: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0" && git push origin v1.0.0

commands.what: Shelves uncommitted work so you can switch branch; pop brings it back.
commands.example: git stash push -m "wip" && git switch main && git stash pop

commands.what: Discards changes in the working tree, or unstages with --staged.
Creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one — the safe way to undo on shared branches (GitOps rollback).
Moves the branch pointer. --soft keeps changes staged, --hard discards them (destructive: local branches only).
Applies one commit from another branch onto the current one, e.g. a fix into a release branch.
Lists and manages remotes. A repository can push to several (origin on GitHub, ado on Azure Repos).
commands.example: git remote add ado https://dev.azure.com/az400edilsonmontry/lab-gitflow/_git/orders-app && git remote -v

commands.what: Lists, creates or deletes branches. -a includes remote branches; -d deletes a merged branch.
Shows who last changed each line and in which commit — useful when investigating a regression.

sections.title: GitHub CLI (gh)
sections.note: GitHub from the terminal: repositories, pull requests, Actions runs, variables, environments and the REST API.

commands.what: Shows which account is signed in and the token scopes. First thing to check when a gh command fails.
Creates a repository; --source with --push publishes an existing local repository.
Clones a repository with the gh credentials.
Opens a pull request from the current branch. --base sets the target; --fill uses the commit messages.
commands.example: gh pr create --base develop --title "Minimum order value" --body "Adds minOrder with tests."

commands.what: Shows the status checks of a PR; --watch waits until they finish.
Merges a PR with the chosen method and can delete the branch.
Shows one PR (with --web in the browser) or lists PRs by state.
Lists workflow runs, filtered by workflow, branch or status.
Shows a run's jobs; --log-failed prints only the failing steps' logs.
Follows a running workflow live, or re-runs a finished one (--failed for failed jobs only).
Starts a workflow_dispatch workflow with inputs.
commands.example: gh workflow run infra.yml -f layer=10-foundation -f action=plan

commands.what: Manages repository (or environment) variables and secrets. Secrets are write-only.
commands.example: gh variable list && gh variable set TF_STATE_RG --body rg-mfs-tfstate

commands.what: Calls any GitHub REST endpoint with your auth — for settings the CLI has no command for.

sections.title: Docker
sections.note: In this lab Docker runs inside WSL Ubuntu; Windows docker works only while WSL is up (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://127.0.0.1:2375).

commands.what: Builds an image from a Dockerfile. -t names and tags it; the last argument is the build context.
Lists local images with tag, ID and size.
Creates and starts a container. -d detached, -p host:container ports, --name, -e environment variables, --rm removes it on exit.
Lists running containers; -a includes stopped ones.
Shows a container's stdout/stderr; -f follows, --tail limits.
Runs a command inside a running container — e.g. a shell to look around.
Stops a container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL) and removes it.
commands.example: docker stop orders && docker rm orders

commands.what: Low-level JSON about a container or image: IP, mounts, env, health. Use --format to pick a field.
Gives an image another name, e.g. the registry path before a push.
Authenticates to a registry and sends or fetches images. For ACR prefer az acr login (Entra ID token, no password).
commands.example: az acr login -n acrmfslab && docker push acrmfslab.azurecr.io/orders:1.0.0

commands.what: Runs a multi-container app from compose.yaml: up -d starts, down stops and removes.
commands.example: docker compose up -d && docker compose logs -f && docker compose down

commands.what: Manages named volumes — data that survives the container.
commands.example: docker volume ls && docker volume inspect orders-data

commands.what: Manages networks; containers on the same user network reach each other by name.
commands.example: docker network create lab && docker run -d --network lab --name db postgres:16

commands.what: Live CPU, memory and I/O per container — first look at a resource problem.
Removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache. -a also removes unused images.
commands.example: docker system df && docker system prune -f

commands.what: Shows the layers of an image and their sizes — useful to shrink images.

sections.title: kubectl
sections.note: In this lab kubectl and minikube run inside WSL; for AKS get credentials first (az aks get-credentials) and kubelogin handles the Entra ID sign-in.

commands.what: Shows and switches contexts (cluster + user + namespace). Check it before any change.
commands.example: kubectl config get-contexts && kubectl config use-context aks-mfs-portal-lab

commands.what: Lists resources. -o wide adds node and IP; -A all namespaces; -w watches changes.
Detailed state plus recent Events — the first stop for Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or ImagePullBackOff.
Container logs; -f follows, --previous shows the crashed container's last logs, -c picks a container.
Creates or updates resources from YAML (declarative). With GitOps, Argo CD does this — use it only in labs.
Deletes resources by name, label or file.
Runs a command in a container, e.g. to test DNS or connectivity from inside the cluster.
Tunnels a local port to a pod or service — reach an app without exposing it.
Status, history, restart and undo of a Deployment rollout. With GitOps, roll back by reverting the commit instead of undo.
Changes the replica count (drift from Git in a GitOps setup — Argo CD will revert it).
CPU and memory per pod or node (needs metrics-server) — to compare usage with requests and limits.
Cluster events in time order: scheduling failures, OOMKilled, failed pulls.
Built-in documentation of any resource field — no browser needed.
Generates YAML for a resource without creating it — a quick start for manifests.
commands.example: kubectl create deployment orders --image=orders:1.0.0 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml

commands.what: Extracts exact fields from the API output for scripts and quick checks.
Checks whether you (or a service account with --as) may perform an action — RBAC troubleshooting.
commands.example: kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n portal-prod

commands.what: Marks a node unschedulable and evicts its pods (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets) for maintenance.
Lists or creates namespaces; -n on every command picks the namespace.
commands.example: kubectl create namespace lab && kubectl get ns
